Planetary science OurBigBook.com
A magnetosphere is the region around a body in which the body's magnetic interaction controls charged-particle motion and its response to the surrounding plasma. A planet with an intrinsic magnetic field can support a compressed dayside and an extended magnetotail in the solar wind. Magnetospheric currents must be distinguished from the internal field when inferring a planetary dynamo.

Magnetosphere OurBigBook.com
An induced magnetosphere is maintained by the interaction of an external magnetized plasma flow with a conducting ionosphere or atmosphere. Its currents and draped magnetic field do not establish an internal planetary dynamo. Venus is a central example; Mars combines this interaction with localized crustal fields.

Planetary magnetic field

Planetary science OurBigBook.com
A planetary magnetic field may include an intrinsic field maintained by an internal planetary dynamo, local crustal remanent magnetization, and externally driven fields associated with the solar wind. Separating these components requires spatial and temporal observations. A global internally sourced field, a localized crustal anomaly, and an induced magnetosphere are different evidence about the planet's present and past interior.

Planetary dynamo

Words: 174 Articles: 2
Planetary magnetic field OurBigBook.com
A planetary dynamo maintains an intrinsic magnetic field by motion of an electrically conducting fluid. The resistive induction equation balances stretching and transport against magnetic diffusion. A sufficiently large magnetic Reynolds number is necessary but does not ensure that the flow regenerates every required field component. Thermal or compositional convection supplies mechanical power; rotation organizes the flow through the Coriolis force, and the Lorentz force density eventually modifies the flow and limits growth. A fluid core can fail to operate a dynamo if it is stably stratified or inadequately driven.

Geodynamo

Words: 63
Planetary dynamo OurBigBook.com
The geodynamo is the maintenance of Earth's magnetic field by electrically conducting fluid motion in its liquid outer core. Rotation and buoyant convection organize helical flow and permit mean-field poloidal–toroidal regeneration. A scalar homogeneous alpha model explains a mechanism and a threshold but omits spherical boundaries, anisotropy, spatial variations and Lorentz force feedback. Reversals and saturation require dynamical or time-dependent transport information beyond a growing constant-coefficient kinematic mode.

Planetary dynamo OurBigBook.com
A geomagnetic reversal changes the large-scale polarity of Earth's intrinsic magnetic field. Crustal remanent magnetization records past reversals. The reversal times are not a regular clock; their occurrence reflects time-dependent dynamo action rather than rigid rotation of a permanent magnet.

Planetary science OurBigBook.com
An asteroid is a small rocky or metallic body orbiting a star. Asteroid dynamics can involve mean-motion resonances, planetary scattering and secular perturbations. Solar-system asteroids illustrate how phase protection can prevent close encounters even when orbital paths approach a planet.

The astronomical unit is a length scale used for Solar System distances, approximately 1.5×1013cm. Coarse estimates sometimes round it to 1013cm. Numerical coefficients in planet formation estimates depend on which approximation is used.

Separation of a planet's materials into compositionally different reservoirs, such as metal-rich core, silicate mantle and crust. A concentrated thin layer of solids can become self-gravitating if particle random velocities and stellar shear do not support it. Gravitational binding is necessary but not sufficient for gas capture. A hydrostatic envelope contracts by losing energy on a Kelvin-Helmholtz scale tKH​∼∣E∣/L. Solid accretion heats it, while radiative transport depends on opacity and convection carries energy when the radiative gradient is unstable. The disk supply and outer tidal/thermal boundaries also matter.

The epoch when the gaseous envelope mass becomes comparable with the solid core mass. Envelope self-gravity then changes structure and can accelerate gas capture through cooling and contraction. A model-dependent threshold beyond which a cooling gaseous envelope cannot remain on a slowly growing low-mass branch around a solid core. A stage in which several neighboring planetary embryos dominate stirring of surrounding planetesimals and grow in a self-regulated manner. Larger embryos heat their feeding populations more strongly, weakening gravitational focusing and preventing unlimited runaway planetesimal growth. A small number of embryos coexist with many much smaller bodies.

The region of a disk from which a planetary embryo can efficiently accrete solids. Its width depends on gravitational encounters and the surrounding orbital population. Approximating that width by a multiple of the Hill radius gives a useful local isolation mass.

The mass reached after consuming an idealized local annulus of solids. A growth regime in which larger planetesimals have shorter fractional growth times. A step-like bend linking relatively less tilted beds on either side. Distributed deformation above a blind fault can produce a monocline without a discrete surface break.
Fold scarp
Words: 24
Folding OurBigBook.com
A topographic step or steepened belt produced by localized folding. It can form above a blind reverse fault without being the trace of the principal fault plane.
Fault-propagation fold
Words: 25
Folding OurBigBook.com
A fold formed as displacement is transferred ahead of a propagating fault tip into surrounding rock. It is one mechanism for surface deformation above a blind reverse fault.
Anticline
Words: 24
Folding OurBigBook.com
A fold with older layers in its core where the age relationships are preserved. Active blind reverse faults can produce asymmetric anticlines and warping of young landforms.
Rock (geology)
Words: 85 Articles: 3
Geology OurBigBook.com
A naturally occurring solid aggregate of minerals or related geological material. Its composition, porosity, cracks and fluid content affect seismic wave speeds and magnetic susceptibility.
Bedrock
Words: 24
Rock (geology) OurBigBook.com
Relatively consolidated rock beneath loose cover. A geophysically defined bedrock interface can be an operational seismic velocity or stiffness boundary and need not coincide with crystalline basement.
Ultramafic rock
Words: 21
Rock (geology) OurBigBook.com
A rock dominated by magnesium- and iron-rich minerals, with lower silica content than typical mafic rocks. Alteration can strongly change its magnetic properties.
Mafic rock
Words: 19
Rock (geology) OurBigBook.com
A rock relatively rich in magnesium- and iron-bearing silicate minerals. Basalt and gabbro are common examples; their magnetic susceptibility depends particularly on magnetic-mineral abundance.

A trapped-charge dating method estimating time since suitable mineral grains last received sufficient light exposure. Continental reconstruction
Words: 31
Paleogeography OurBigBook.com
An inferred arrangement of continental blocks at a specified geological time. Relative rotations must satisfy independent constraints from paleomagnetism, stratigraphy, sedimentary provenance, metamorphic belts and dated suture zones. Geometric compatibility alone does not establish uniqueness.
Columbia (supercontinent)
Words: 49
Paleogeography OurBigBook.com
An early Proterozoic supercontinent whose assembly is commonly placed broadly around 1.9–1.6 billion years ago. The terms Columbia and Nuna are often used interchangeably, although some reconstructions distinguish their regional or temporal meanings. Geological connections and dated apparent polar wander paths test proposed configurations.[ref]
Rodinia
Words: 38
Paleogeography OurBigBook.com
A Proterozoic supercontinent assembled principally around 1.1–0.9 billion years ago and dispersed in stages later in the Proterozoic. Its detailed continental configuration is less tightly constrained than that of Pangaea, because later deformation and recycling have removed much of the original evidence.
Pangaea
Words: 25
Paleogeography OurBigBook.com
The supercontinent assembled by the late Paleozoic and fragmented during the Mesozoic. Restored geological belts, fossil assemblages, glacial deposits, paleomagnetism and the younger seafloor spreading record provide complementary constraints on its history.
Continental configuration
Words: 12
Paleogeography OurBigBook.com
The positions, shapes and connections of continental regions at a specified time.
Paleoenvironment
Words: 10
Geology OurBigBook.com
A reconstructed past environment, inferred from geological and biological evidence.
Structural geology
Words: 421 Articles: 16
Geology OurBigBook.com
Study of deformation and the geometry and history of geological structures.
Lithological contact
Words: 36
Structural geology OurBigBook.com
A boundary between bodies with different lithologies. It can be depositional, intrusive or created by faulting. A remotely observed colour change is evidence for a candidate lithological contact, but illumination, soil and vegetation changes require independent checks.
Mineral vein
Words: 113 Articles: 1
Structural geology OurBigBook.com
A fracture filled by minerals precipitated from a fluid. Quartz and calcite are common examples. Growth textures and cross-cutting relations can constrain opening and fluid-flow history, but mineral filling alone does not establish whether the fracture also experienced fault slip.
Hydraulic opening of a mineral vein (Pf​>σn​+T0​)
Words: 77
Mineral vein OurBigBook.com
A fluid-filled fracture can open perpendicular to the least compressive principal stress. In a compression-positive contact approximation, effective stress is σn′​=σn​−Pf​. Opening an initially intact plane of tensile strength T0​ requires
σn​−Pf​<−T0​.
(3)
A sufficiently weak pre-existing crack can open near zero effective compression. Increasing isotropic pore fluid pressure translates all effective principal stresses without rotating their directions, so an opening fracture and a frictional normal fault can record compatible stress axes at different pressure episodes. Subsequent mineral precipitation creates a mineral vein; white appearance alone does not identify its filling mineral.
Geological joint
Words: 45
Structural geology OurBigBook.com
An opening fracture in rock with little or no shear displacement across its faces. A geological joint is approximately normal to the least compressive principal stress when it forms in a homogeneous medium. It can remain open or become a mineral vein. Unlike a fault, a geological joint need not contain crushed fault rock.
Ductile deformation
Words: 32
Structural geology OurBigBook.com
Distributed permanent change of shape without requiring a discrete through-going brittle rupture. Its mechanisms and rate depend on temperature, stress, composition and timescale; deep ductile structures need not be active earthquake faults.
Tectonic shortening
Words: 25
Structural geology OurBigBook.com
Reduction of distance between material markers during tectonic deformation. Folding, reverse faulting and distributed strain can accommodate it; the shortening direction alone does not determine all three principal stresses.
Shear sense
Words: 14
Structural geology OurBigBook.com
The relative movement direction across a shear zone, inferred from appropriately interpreted structural indicators.
Fold
Words: 12
Structural geology OurBigBook.com
A bend in originally more nearly planar geological layering or other surfaces.
Thrust belt

Structural geology OurBigBook.com
A region of contractional deformation dominated by linked thrust faults and associated folds.
Mountain building

Construction of elevated mountain regions through crustal thickening, magmatic addition or other tectonic processes.

An elongated region affected by mountain building, commonly containing related thrust belts, metamorphic belts and deformed sedimentary successions. Restoring its age and internal structure across separated continental blocks can test continental reconstruction.
Andes
Words: 16

The mountain system along western South America, associated with subduction and a spatially variable history of crustal shortening.
Tectonic uplift
Words: 21

An increase in rock or surface elevation caused by tectonic processes; rock uplift and surface uplift can differ because of erosion.
Mélange
Words: 18
Structural geology OurBigBook.com
A heterogeneous geological body containing blocks within a deformed matrix; formation can involve tectonic, sedimentary or mixed processes.
Tectonic exhumation
Words: 15
Structural geology OurBigBook.com
Return of formerly buried rock toward the surface through tectonic deformation, often aided by erosion.
Tectonic reworking

Structural geology OurBigBook.com
Modification of pre-existing rocks and structures during subsequent tectonic events.
Sedimentology
Words: 360 Articles: 15
Geology OurBigBook.com
Study of sediments, their transport, deposition and subsequent modification.
Sedimentary facies
Words: 40
Sedimentology OurBigBook.com
A distinguishable set of properties of a sedimentary deposit, including composition, grain size, structures and biological contents, interpreted in relation to its depositional environment. Spatial and vertical changes among sedimentary facies help reconstruct a paleoenvironment; no single property invariably identifies a unique setting.
Aggradation
Words: 19
Sedimentology OurBigBook.com
Rise of a depositional surface through net sediment accumulation. It can fill a hanging-wall basin and conceal an active fault scarp.
Sedimentary basin
Words: 24
Sedimentology OurBigBook.com
A region of long-term accommodation and accumulation of sediments, commonly associated with subsidence. Its gravity anomaly depends on geometry and the geophysical density contrast between fill and surrounding rock.
Sedimentary provenance
Words: 37 Articles: 1
Sedimentology OurBigBook.com
The source and transport history of sediments, inferred from composition, mineral ages and geological relationships.
Detrital zircon
Words: 22
Sedimentary provenance OurBigBook.com
A zircon grain eroded from its source and deposited as a sedimentary particle. Its crystallization age can precede deposition by a long interval.
Sedimentary deposit
Words: 231 Articles: 9
Sedimentology OurBigBook.com
An accumulation of deposited sediments or precipitated sedimentary material.
Limestone
Words: 34
Sedimentary deposit OurBigBook.com
A sedimentary rock composed mainly of calcium carbonate, commonly calcite. Many limestones form through biological or chemical carbonate accumulation in marine settings, while others form in lakes. Burial, cementation, dissolution and fractures can strongly alter their porosity and porous permeability.
Glacial deposit
Words: 40
Sedimentary deposit OurBigBook.com
Material deposited directly by ice or by associated meltwater. Its sedimentary facies, transport directions and age constrain a former glacial paleoenvironment. Correlating such deposits across continents can test continental reconstruction, but requires distinguishing the original depositional record from later transport and deformation.
Colluvium
Words: 57 Articles: 1
Sedimentary deposit OurBigBook.com
Slope-derived sediments transported chiefly by gravity and local slope processes. Collapse and raveling of an earthquake fault scarp can supply a colluvial wedge.
Colluvial wedge

Colluvium OurBigBook.com
A wedge-shaped slope deposit, commonly thickest beside a scarp and thinning away from it. When combined with faulting, burial and cross-cutting relations it can record a past surface-rupturing earthquake; a wedge alone does not prove a separate event.
Alluvium
Words: 25
Sedimentary deposit OurBigBook.com
Loose sediments transported and deposited by flowing water, such as channel or floodplain material. Their strength, saturation and thickness affect how a buried fault ruptures the surface.
Evaporite
Words: 16
Sedimentary deposit OurBigBook.com
A deposit formed by precipitation of dissolved substances as a solution becomes concentrated, commonly by evaporation.
Mudstone
Words: 8
Sedimentary deposit OurBigBook.com
Fine-grained sedimentary rock composed predominantly of mud-sized particles.
River delta
Words: 28
Sedimentary deposit OurBigBook.com
A depositional body built where a sediment-bearing river enters a more slowly moving body of water. Its internal structure and basin context distinguish it from other fan-shaped deposits.
Lacustrine deposit
Words: 15
Sedimentary deposit OurBigBook.com
A deposit formed in a lake. Fine lacustrine deposits can archive past water chemistry and preserve organic matter.

Geology OurBigBook.com
Study of rocks, their formation and their transformations.

Petrology OurBigBook.com
A rock formed by crystallization of magma or lava. Intrusive bodies crystallize below the surface, while extrusive rocks solidify at or near the surface. Granite is a common intrusive example and basalt a common extrusive example.

Words: 38
Igneous rock OurBigBook.com
An igneous rock composed predominantly of plagioclase. Lunar anorthositic rocks are central to the flotation interpretation of the lunar magma ocean. Their mineral and chemical composition does not alone date the formation of the complete crustal layer; sample context and radiometric dating are needed.
Lithology
Words: 31
Petrology OurBigBook.com
The observable physical and compositional character of rock, including its constituent minerals, texture and grain size. Different lithologies can have distinct spectral reflectance, density and magnetic susceptibility, making geological mapping possible through several independent measurements.

Words: 16

Fine fragmented material produced by a volcanic eruption; dispersal can affect regions far from the vent.

A rock formed through accumulation of crystals separated from magma, often during fractional crystallization.
Tonalite
Words: 15

An intrusive rock containing quartz and predominantly plagioclase rather than alkali feldspar; it is one member of tonalite-trondhjemite-granodiorite.

Words: 16 Articles: 1
Petrology OurBigBook.com
A felsic volcanic rock broadly corresponding in bulk composition to granite.

Volcanism producing rhyolite or liquids of similar felsic composition.
Dacite

Petrology OurBigBook.com
A silica-rich volcanic rock, compositionally between typical andesite and rhyolite.
Andesite
Words: 8
Petrology OurBigBook.com
A volcanic rock with intermediate composition, common in volcanic arcs.

An ultramafic volcanic rock whose inferred magnesium-rich parental liquids constrain high-temperature mantle melting; mantle plume and ambient mantle interpretations must be distinguished.

A texture with elongate or skeletal crystals, commonly olivine, in some ultramafic lavas. It records crystal growth and cooling conditions and supports interpretation of a lava's crystallization history. It is not alone a numerical thermometer for ambient mantle potential temperature.
Diorite

Petrology OurBigBook.com
A coarse-grained intrusive rock with intermediate composition, commonly containing plagioclase and amphibole or pyroxene.
Metamorphic rock
Words: 101 Articles: 6
Petrology OurBigBook.com
Rock transformed by changes in temperature, pressure, deformation or fluid conditions while predominantly remaining solid.
Greenstone
Words: 35
Metamorphic rock OurBigBook.com
A common descriptive name for low-grade metamorphosed mafic volcanic rock, often containing greenish minerals. A greenstone belt can contain these rocks together with other volcanic and sedimentary rocks; the belt name does not imply uniform composition or density.
Gneiss

A metamorphic rock with compositional banding; its bulk composition can be felsic, intermediate or mafic.
Metasedimentary rock
Words: 5
Metamorphic rock OurBigBook.com
A metamorphic rock formed from a sedimentary rock precursor.

A high-grade metamorphic rock with an assemblage characteristic of granulite facies; both felsic and mafic examples occur.
Mafic granulite

A mafic rock with a granulite-facies assemblage. Granulite alone specifies a metamorphic facies, not the mafic composition.
Amphibolite

A metamorphic rock dominated by amphibole and plagioclase, commonly derived from a mafic precursor.
Granodiorite
Words: 14
Petrology OurBigBook.com
A coarse-grained intrusive rock containing quartz and feldspar, with more plagioclase relative to alkali feldspar than typical granite.
Granite
Words: 8
Petrology OurBigBook.com
A coarse-grained felsic intrusive rock, rich in quartz and feldspar.
Sedimentary rock
Words: 29 Articles: 1
Petrology OurBigBook.com
Rock formed through deposition and subsequent consolidation or precipitation of material at or near a planetary surface.
Sandstone
Words: 13
Sedimentary rock OurBigBook.com
A sedimentary rock composed predominantly of sand-sized grains. Cementation, porosity, pore fluid and effective stress strongly affect its seismic velocity.
Mafic
Words: 13
Petrology OurBigBook.com
A compositional description for magnesium- and iron-rich silicate material; basalt and gabbro are common mafic rocks.
Felsic

A compositional description for rocks or magma rich in silica and commonly feldspar and quartz, contrasting with mafic compositions.

A family of felsic plutonic rocks prominent in studies of early continental crust. Melting hydrous mafic sources can generate related compositions, but the rock name alone does not establish subduction.
Blueschist

Petrology OurBigBook.com
Metamorphic rock containing characteristic blue amphibole, associated with some low-temperature, high-pressure assemblages.
Eclogite

Petrology OurBigBook.com
High-pressure metamorphic rock with a major assemblage of garnet and omphacitic clinopyroxene, generally lacking plagioclase. It can derive from mafic crust by several burial mechanisms.
Serpentinite

Petrology OurBigBook.com
Rock dominated by serpentine minerals, commonly produced by serpentinization of ultramafic rock.
Pyroxenite

Petrology OurBigBook.com
An ultramafic rock dominated by pyroxenes; it can originate through several magmatic and reactive processes.
Peridotite

An ultramafic rock dominated by olivine with pyroxenes and other phases, abundant in the upper mantle.
Harzburgite

An ultramafic rock dominated by olivine and orthopyroxene; strongly melt-depleted mantle commonly has this composition.

Modification of a magma by incorporation or assimilation of surrounding crust.

Progressive separation of crystals from a melt, changing the composition of the residual liquid.

Melting of only part of a rock; the melt and remaining solid generally have different compositions.

Chemical modification of residual rock by extraction of melt. In mantle peridotite, depletion commonly changes mineral proportions and trace-element contents, and can accompany volatile loss. Transformation of suitable rock to an eclogite assemblage. Increased density can affect slab buoyancy, but reaction kinetics can delay transformation.

An elongated region characterized by a related metamorphic history or assemblage distribution.

Metamorphism at elevated pressure relative to ordinary shallow-crustal environments; its tectonic meaning depends on the full pressure-temperature-time path.
Ultrahigh-pressure metamorphism

Metamorphism reaching conditions sufficient for diagnostic high-pressure phases such as coesite in an appropriate composition. Their growth must be distinguished from detrital inheritance or unrelated inclusions.

Words: 27
Metamorphism OurBigBook.com
The inferred history of pressure and temperature experienced by a rock. Dating specific growth domains and linking them to mineral reactions are needed to attach time to the path.
Decarbonation
Words: 13

A reaction that consumes carbonate-bearing assemblages and releases carbon dioxide or another carbon-bearing fluid component.
Metasomatism

Explanations assigning major geological changes to exceptional or rapid events. This does not logically entail that every formation was produced by one biblical flood.
Uniformitarianism

A family of geological commitments involving explanation by observable processes and continuity of natural laws. Continuity of laws must be distinguished from the stronger claim that every process always acts at an unchanging rate.
Deep time

Geological time extending far beyond ordinary human historical timescales. Arguments from the ordering of many processes can support long durations without providing a modern radiometric age.

Study of the succession and relationships of rock layers. A relative sequence of deposition and disturbance does not by itself give an absolute numerical age.

A distinguishable layer within a soil profile formed by soil processes. A buried horizon can mark a stable former surface and help separate phases of deposition and fault slip.

Lunar phase

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Moon OurBigBook.com
A lunar phase is the appearance of the sunlit portion of the Moon as seen from Earth. Outside a lunar eclipse, the distant Sun illuminates approximately one hemisphere of the Moon, but an observer sees a changing overlap of that hemisphere with the hemisphere facing Earth. The lunar phase therefore changes even though synchronous rotation keeps approximately the same near side of the Moon facing Earth. [ref].
The cycle runs through new Moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full Moon, waning gibbous, last quarter and waning crescent. “Waxing” means that the lunar illuminated fraction is increasing; “waning” means it is decreasing. A crescent has less than half its apparent disk sunlit, and a gibbous lunar phase has more than half. First and last quarter each show half a disk: “quarter” refers to progress around the cycle, rather than a quarter of the disk being lit. [ref].
An instructive circular orbit model puts Earth at the origin, the Sun far away along +x, and the Moon at R(cosθ,sinθ). The sunward position x>0, θ=0, gives new Moon; the opposite position x<0, θ=π, gives full Moon. Counterclockwise motion gives first quarter at θ=π/2 and last quarter at θ=3π/2. The Sun's direction is fixed during this snapshot of the cycle. Every small globe in the orbital view is illuminated on its +x half; the adjacent apparent disks are separate views from Earth, rather than globes viewed from above.
The disk views choose north up, with the upward direction perpendicular to the orbital plane. In this convention waxing lunar phases are bright on the right and waning lunar phases on the left. Local horizon orientation and viewing from different locations on Earth can rotate the apparent disk; its lit edge always points toward the projected direction of the Sun. The lunar illuminated fraction is unaffected by this rotation.
The useful angle is the phase angle α=∠SME, with S the Sun, M the Moon and E the observer at Earth's center: its vertex is at the Moon. Full Moon has α=0, quarter has α=π/2, and new Moon has α=π in the ideal model. By contrast, the elongation ϵ=∠SEM has its vertex at Earth. For a distant Sun, its rays are parallel, so
α=π−ϵ,k=21+cosα​=21−cosϵ​.
(4)
Here k is the lunar illuminated fraction: a fraction of projected disk area, not a fraction of the Moon's total surface area or its received radiant flux relative to full Moon. The phase angle and unsigned elongation each lie between 0 and π, so either alone gives the illuminated amount without distinguishing waxing from waning. The orbital direction resolves that ambiguity.
The lunar illuminated fraction has an elegant geometric derivation. Model the Moon as a sphere of unit radius and view it along the z direction. Take the Sun's unit direction to be (sinα,0,cosα). A visible surface point above apparent disk coordinates (x,y) has z=1−x2−y2​. Direct illumination requires the outward normal's dot product with the sunward direction to be positive. The day-night terminator therefore obeys xsinα+zcosα=0. At a fixed y, set q=1−y2​; the visible day-night terminator is xt​=−qcosα, and the illuminated strip extends from xt​ to the right edge q. Integrating its width gives
Alit​=∫−11​(1+cosα)1−y2​dy=2π​(1+cosα),k=πAlit​​.
(5)
The integral is the area of half a unit circle. Thus a three-dimensional visibility problem reduces to a circle's area and a cosine. The derivation assumes parallel sunlight, a distant observer and a sphere, and ignores a lunar eclipse. Real observed brightness additionally depends on surface scattering of light and observing geometry, so k=1/2 does not promise half the full-Moon radiant flux.
For a worked example, elongation ϵ=60∘ gives phase angle α=120∘ and k=(1+cos120∘)/2=1/4: a crescent with 25% of its apparent disk sunlit. At elongation 120∘, the phase angle is 60∘ and k=3/4: a gibbous lunar phase. At 90∘, k=1/2. In each case the same k occurs once while waxing and once while waning in the ideal cycle.
Ordinary lunar phases are not caused by Earth's shadow. A lunar eclipse occurs only when the Moon actually enters that shadow near full Moon. The orbital inclination of the Moon is about 5∘ relative to Earth's orbital plane around the Sun; most full Moons pass above or below the shadow. This is why full Moon does not imply a lunar eclipse every month. [ref].
The phase cycle is a synodic month, about 29.5 days, whereas the Moon's orbital period relative to distant stars is a sidereal month, about 27.3 days. During one sidereal month, Earth advances around the Sun, so the Moon must move farther to repeat the sunward alignment. For coplanar circular orbits traversed in the same direction, subtract their mean motions: nsyn​=nsid​−nyear​, with n=2π/P. Hence
Psyn​1​=Psid​1​−Pyear​1​,Psyn​=Pyear​−Psid​Psid​Pyear​​.
(6)
Using Psid​=27.321661days and Pyear​=365.256days gives Psyn​=29.530591days, consistent with the mean synodic month of 29.53059 days. After one sidereal month, the sunward direction has advanced about 26.93∘; catching up takes about 2.21 more days. These are mean-period estimates: orbital eccentricity and changing geometry make individual synodic months vary. [ref]. [ref].
The lunar phase is also a practical clock for observing. Full Moon is opposite the Sun and rises roughly at sunset; first quarter is about a right angle from the Sun and is convenient in the evening, while last quarter is convenient before dawn. These are rough guides, not exact rise-time predictions for every place and season. [ref]. Historically, repeated lunar phases provided the month in lunar calendars, while half-lit disks gave Aristarchus of Samos a way to infer astronomical distances. [ref].

Keeping the Sun at a finite distance, let dEM​ and dES​ be the distances from Earth to the Moon and Sun. Then elongation ϵ at Earth gives
cosϵ=dES​dEM​​,dEM​dES​​=cosϵ1​.
(7)

The example shows how lunar phase geometry becomes a distance measurement, but the ratio is extremely sensitive to an angle close to 90∘. Unlike the distant-Sun approximation, this finite triangle has elongation slightly less than 90∘ at half illumination. [ref].

Moon OurBigBook.com
A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth blocks some or all of the direct sunlight reaching the Moon. It requires alignment near full Moon; the orbital inclination usually carries the Moon clear of Earth's shadow. Ordinary lunar phases instead arise from viewing different amounts of the sunlit hemisphere. [ref].

Libration

Words: 88
Moon OurBigBook.com
Libration is the apparent rocking of a body as seen by an observer. For the Moon, longitudinal libration arises because orbital eccentricity makes its orbital angular speed vary while its spin is much more uniform: the direction to Earth advances ahead of, then falls behind, the mean facing direction. The Moon's tilted geometry also causes latitudinal libration; small actual rotational oscillations provide further corrections. Thus lunar synchronous rotation holds in the mean, rather than requiring exact instantaneous alignment. [ref]. [ref].

The wake's force back on the object produces dynamical friction.

Isotropic stellar mass loss OurBigBook.com
Suppose an initially circular Kepler orbit of radius R surrounds central mass M, and a fraction 0<f<1/2 is removed quickly compared with the orbital period. Assume no recoil or wind drag, so the satellite's position and velocity are continuous through the change. Its specific angular momentum stays GMR​, while its new specific orbital energy is −GM(1−2f)/(2R). The resulting elliptic Kepler orbit has semi-major axis a=(1−f)R/(1−2f), pericentre rp​=R, apocentre ra​=R/(1−2f) and orbital eccentricity e=f/(1−f). The limiting loss fraction f=1/2 gives a parabolic Kepler orbit; larger losses unbind the initially circular satellite. Slow removal instead produces adiabatic orbital expansion under isotropic mass loss, which preserves circularity to leading adiabatic order.

Tidal locking

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Planetary system dynamics OurBigBook.com
Tidal locking settles a body's spin into a sustained relation with its orbital motion through tidal forces and tidal dissipation. The simplest case is synchronous rotation, a 1:1 spin-orbit resonance. On an ideal circular orbit, with spin axis perpendicular to the orbital plane, the body keeps the same face toward its companion, as the Moon approximately does toward Earth. [ref].
This article retains the broader sense of tidal locking as capture into a spin-orbit resonance; the term is also commonly used specifically for synchronous rotation. Tidally evolved rotation need not be 1:1: Mercury has a 3:2 spin-orbit resonance with the Sun, turning three times in two orbital periods. The distinction matters when inferring illumination or climate from a spin period. [ref].

Tidal deformation

Words: 76
Tidal locking OurBigBook.com
Tidal deformation is the change in a body's shape caused by differential gravity across it, that is, by a tidal force. The familiar two-bulge picture represents an elongated response along the companion direction, rather than a separate force pulling only the nearest surface. If spin and orbital motion differ, the forcing sweeps through the body's material. With tidal dissipation, the response is out of alignment with the instantaneous forcing, allowing a net torque. [ref].

Secular tidal torque (⟨τ⟩)

Words: 186
Tidal locking OurBigBook.com
A secular tidal torque is the torque remaining after averaging the changing tidal interaction over fast orbital and rotational motion. The misaligned tidal deformation lets the companion's gravity change the spin angular momentum; the orbit receives the opposite torque. Tidal dissipation converts mechanical energy into heat, while total angular momentum is conserved in an isolated system. Thus the spin-orbit coupling exchanges angular momentum rather than destroying it. [ref].
For intuition near synchronous rotation on a circular orbit, hold mean motion n and moment of inertia I fixed and adopt the illustrative linear dissipative law
Iω˙=⟨τ⟩=−K(ω−n),K>0,ω=θ˙.
(8)
Here ω is spin angular velocity, θ is a marked surface direction in an inertial frame, and K is a response coefficient, not a universal material constant. A faster spin is slowed and a slower prograde spin is accelerated. The solution and the associated mechanical power loss are
ω(t)−n=[ω(0)−n]e−Kt/I,E˙mech​=⟨τ⟩(ω−n)=−K(ω−n)2≤0.
(9)
The orbital contribution to this power is −n⟨τ⟩, and the spin contribution is ω⟨τ⟩; their sum becomes heat. Holding n fixed is a local approximation to the coupled evolution. Actual secular tidal torque depends on the deformation response and orbital eccentricity, so this simple law does not establish which spin-orbit resonance an eccentric body captures into.

Spin-orbit resonance (⟨ω⟩/n=p/q)

Words: 81
Tidal locking OurBigBook.com
A prograde spin-orbit resonance relates mean spin angular velocity to mean motion by a ratio of small positive integers, ⟨ω⟩/n=p/q: the body makes p turns in q orbital periods. Synchronous rotation is 1:1; Mercury's 3:2 spin-orbit resonance is nonsynchronous. The relevant combination of spin and orbital angles must stay bounded around a preferred orientation, not merely have a near-integer frequency ratio. For an elongated body on an eccentric orbit, the companion's gravitational torque on the permanent shape can sustain the resonance while tidal dissipation permits capture. [ref].

Synchronous rotation

Words: 636 Articles: 2
Tidal locking OurBigBook.com
Synchronous rotation means one prograde turn about the body's own axis per orbital period, measured against fixed directions in an inertial frame. This 1:1 spin-orbit resonance approximately describes the Moon's synchronous rotation toward Earth. [ref].
The striking geometric idea is that one turn in space can keep one face toward the companion: a fixed orientation in the frame turning with the orbit is a changing orientation in an inertial frame. This distinction helps us predict illumination: a synchronously rotating exoplanet orbiting its illuminating star can have persistent day and night hemispheres, whereas the Moon, synchronized to Earth, receives changing illumination from a different body, the Sun.
Facing geometry of synchronous rotation (θ−f=constant)
Words: 146
Synchronous rotation OurBigBook.com
View a circular orbit along its perpendicular spin axis. Let f be the orbital angle measured from a fixed direction, choosing an arbitrary zero for the circular limit of true anomaly, and let θ be the direction of an outward arrow painted on the body, measured from the same fixed direction. The direction from the body to its companion is f+π. Thus an inward-facing arrow satisfies
θ=f+π(mod2π),θ˙=f˙​=n,n=T2π​.
(10)
More generally synchronous rotation keeps θ−f constant; its particular value selects which surface direction faces the companion. Over one orbital period T, both f and the unwrapped θ increase by 2π. This is the short geometric explanation for one turn per orbit. For a nonspinning body, θ˙=0 instead, and the companion direction sweeps through all surface longitudes. On an eccentric orbit, mean 1:1 spin does not force θ−f to stay exactly constant: true anomaly advances nonuniformly, producing the longitudinal component of libration.
Illumination of a synchronously rotating moon
Words: 316
Synchronous rotation OurBigBook.com
Facing a companion and facing the source of light are different relations. The Moon keeps its near side of the Moon approximately toward Earth, while the direction to the distant Sun is nearly fixed during the idealized orbit shown below. A fixed surface patch therefore turns toward, across and away from sunlight. The far side of the Moon has day and night too; its name does not mean permanent darkness. [ref].
If the Sun direction has fixed angle α and the marked surface patch has outward normal vector at angle θ, its direct illumination is proportional to max(0,cos(θ−α)). With synchronous rotation, θ=f+π, so the patch goes through day and night even though it always faces Earth. In reality the Earth-Moon system advances around the Sun: the lunar spin and orbital cycle relative to distant stars is about 27.3 Earth days, while the lunar phase cycle has a synodic period of about 29.5 Earth days. These numbers describe the actual system, not the fixed-sunlight cartoon. [ref].
For a synchronously rotating exoplanet whose orbital companion is itself the illuminating star, the direction to the star turns with the orbit. On an ideal circular orbit, with perpendicular spin axis and no additional oscillations, this direction is fixed relative to the surface, giving persistent day and night hemispheres. Day-night heat redistribution then helps determine the nightside temperature; permanent lack of direct starlight does not imply zero temperature. Orbital eccentricity and departures from this ideal spin geometry modify that simple picture.

Planetary system dynamics OurBigBook.com
Tidal heating converts mechanical energy of tidal deformation into internal heat through tidal dissipation. Sustained orbital eccentricity or a spin axis tilted relative to the orbital plane's perpendicular can maintain changing tidal deformation and heat an exoplanet interior. Thus synchronous rotation alone does not eliminate tidal heating.

Tidal heating OurBigBook.com
Tidal dissipation converts mechanical energy associated with a time-varying tidal deformation into heat. It can reduce orbital eccentricity, drive synchronous rotation, and contribute deep planetary heating. A circular orbit with exact synchronous rotation, perpendicular spin axis and no additional forcing has a static tidal deformation in the body's frame and need not sustain substantial tidal heating.

Interplanetary dust

Interplanetary dust consists of small solid particles orbiting within a planetary system and responding to gravity, radiation, plasma, and collisions.

A dust tail is an extended distribution of grains released from a localized moving source. Radiation pressure changes the grains' orbits; their release times, grain properties and survival probabilities determine the spatial profile.

The radiation-pressure efficiency is the radiation-force cross-section of a grain divided by its geometric cross-section. It is of order unity for grains larger than the illuminating wavelength and depends strongly on size and composition in the small-particle regime.

A grain released from a circular parent orbit without a relative velocity impulse is unbound when radiation pressure reduces the effective stellar attraction sufficiently. For β>1, the effective inverse-square force is repulsive.
Radiation-pressure blowout threshold (β=1/2)

Radiation-pressure blowout orbit OurBigBook.com
The zero-kick circular-parent threshold is β=1/2: below it grains are initially bound, at it their conservative release orbit is parabolic, and above it they are initially unbound. Poynting–Robertson drag can modify a marginal orbit, so the threshold is a statement about the instantaneous release orbit, not an exact capture criterion with dissipation included.

Poynting–Robertson drag is the tangential component of stellar radiation force caused by aberration in an orbiting dust grain's frame. It removes orbital energy and angular momentum and drives the grain inward.

Grains therefore arrive in increasing diameter order. This model of Poynting–Robertson drag assumes nearly circular Kepler orbits, fixed positive γ, and no grain loss or diameter changes before arrival. At a positive time, the map is monotone in D and allows the initial power-law size distribution to be transformed into a spatial distribution or an arrival-time distribution.

During inward migration, dust can be captured into an exterior mean-motion resonance with a planet. A phase-shifted conjunction then lets planetary torque replace angular momentum lost to Poynting–Robertson drag.

Given e˙=−Csinϕ−Ae and ϖ˙=(C/e)cosϕ, the leading Keplerian detuning gives ϕ˙​=−Bx−(C/e)cosϕ. Differentiating z and using eiϕ(sinϕ+icosϕ)=i proves the displayed equation. True longitude adds a fast orbital ripple and does not yield this autonomous averaged equation directly.

Balancing the two dissipative rates gives ef2​=2/[5(p+1)], sinϕf​=−Aef​/C and Bxf​=−(C/ef​)cosϕf​. Two fixed points exist when A<C5(p+1)/2​. The negative-cosine branch has xf​>0 and is stable in this leading model: a phase increase raises the positive resonant torque, raises semi-major axis, lowers mean motion, and reverses the phase drift. The positive-cosine branch has the opposite feedback.
For a coupled verification put z=u+iv. The characteristic polynomial at either fixed point is λ3+2Aλ2+[A2+B2xf2​−2B(p+1)Cuf​]λ−4AB(p+1)Cuf​. For uf​<0 its positive coefficients satisfy the cubic Routh-Hurwitz stability criterion, since the remaining inequality reduces to 2A(A2+B2xf2​)>0. For uf​>0 its negative constant term forces a positive real root. At the equality threshold the equilibria merge and an eigenvalue is zero. This is local stability for the frozen smooth-coefficient approximation, not a conclusion for arbitrary rapidly varying dissipation laws.

At pericentre, mean longitude equals longitude of periapsis, so resonant argument ϕ=(p+q)λ−pλp​−qϖ becomes ϕ=p(ϖ−λp​). The pericentre angle in the planet's rotating frame is ϕ/p modulo 2π/p. For coprime p,q, there are p distinct pericentre directions before the trajectory closes. Resonant-argument libration restricts these directions and supplies resonance protection.
